notes.b: Fish is prepared according to its shape and type, so that it cooks evenly, looks good and is safe to eat. The steps differ for whole fish, fillets and shellfish.
points: Whole round fish is scaled, gutted and washed before cooking; the head, tail and fins may be removed or trimmed. Flat fish may be skinned.
Fillets are cut away from the bones. Leaving the skin on helps a delicate fillet hold its shape during cooking, because the skin keeps the flakes together.
Mussels are scrubbed and the beards (the stringy threads that stick out of the shell) removed. Any mussel that stays open when tapped is discarded, because it is probably dead and unsafe.
After cooking, any mussel that has not opened is discarded too. Prawns are cooked until they turn pink, which shows they are done.

Wash and dry fish before cooking, and keep raw fish, and the board and knife used for it, apart from cooked food, so that bacteria from the raw fish do not spread to food that will not be cooked again.
notes.tip: Fish is cooked when the flesh turns opaque and flakes easily. Don't wait for it to be dry, or it will be overcooked.

notes.b: Fish needs less cooking than meat, and the effects of heat are fast and easy to overdo. Examiners ask for a list of four or five effects, so each one below is a separate fact.
points: Coagulation: the protein in the flesh sets, so raw translucent flesh turns opaque and firm.
Flaking: the thin connective tissue between the muscle fibres changes to gelatine and breaks down quickly, so the flesh separates into flakes. This is why fish cooks fast.
Overcooking toughens the protein and dries out the flesh, because the protein shrinks and squeezes the moisture out.
Micro-organisms (bacteria) and parasites are killed, so well-cooked fish is safe to eat.
Heat changes the protein so that it is easier to digest, and flavour develops during cooking.
Some B vitamins and minerals dissolve into the cooking liquid or are lost by heat. The liquid can be used in a sauce or soup to keep them. Fat-soluble vitamins are mostly kept.
Oily fish loses some fat into the pan or grill, while white fish absorbs fat if it is fried.
notes.tip: Don't say the connective tissue toughens: in fish it turns to gelatine and the flesh flakes. It is the overcooked protein that toughens. Make sure your list includes protein setting and turning opaque, flaking, overcooking toughening, microbes killed, flavour and digestibility, and B vitamins and minerals lost to the cooking liquid.

notes.b: Every cooking method moves heat into the food in one of four ways. Knowing which one applies is how you state the underlying principle of a method.
points: Conduction: heat passes from molecule to molecule through a solid or a liquid in contact with the food, e.g. the pan on the hob, or the fat in shallow frying.
Convection: heat is carried through circulating liquid, steam or hot air, in which the hotter material rises and cooler material falls, e.g. poaching, steaming, baking, stewing and deep frying.
Radiation: infrared heat travels in rays from the heat source straight to the surface of the food, e.g. grilling and barbecuing.
Microwave: electromagnetic waves make the water molecules in the food vibrate, which generates heat inside the food, so cooking is quick.
notes.tip: Radiation is the principle for grilling; convection and conduction are the principles for poaching. Don't say grilling is conduction.

notes.b: Poaching is the standard moist method for fish, because the gentle heat cooks the flesh without breaking it up.
points: How it is done: fish is cooked gently in liquid (water, milk, stock or wine) just below simmering point, about 85 °C (80-90 °C), in a saucepan on the hob or in a covered dish in the oven.
Principle: conduction and convection through the liquid. The gentle heat cooks the fish without breaking up the delicate flesh.
Result: poached fish is moist, easy to digest and keeps its shape, but it may lack flavour, so it is usually served with a sauce.
Poaching is a good method for delicate white fish and for salmon.
Boiling vigorously breaks up the flesh and loses flavour and nutrients, so fish is simmered or poached instead.
notes.tip: For a question on one moist method and its principle, poaching with convection and conduction is a safe answer. The scheme also accepts boiling, simmering, steaming and stewing, but recommend poaching or steaming, and say that vigorous boiling is unsuitable.

notes.b: Steaming and stewing are two more moist methods. Both keep the nutrients, because they use little or no water that is thrown away.
points: Steaming: food is cooked by steam rising from boiling water, either between two plates over a saucepan, in a covered bowl standing in boiling water, or in a steamer.
Steaming principle: convection, with the heat released as the steam condenses on the food.
Steamed fish is light and easily digested, has a mild flavour, loses few nutrients and has no fat added.
Stewing or casserole cooking: food is cooked slowly in liquid in a covered container on the hob or in the oven, by convection and conduction.
Stewing suits fish stews, chowders and fish in sauce. The liquid is eaten, so the nutrients that dissolve into it are kept.
notes.tip: If asked for a moist method with its principle, steaming (convection) is a good alternative to poaching. State how it is done as well as the principle.

notes.b: Grilling and barbecuing both cook by radiant heat, with no liquid, so they are dry methods that suit fish.
points: Grilling: food is cooked by radiant heat under the grill. The heat seals the surface, retaining flavour, moisture and nutrients.
Grilled fish is quick to cook and needs little fat, but it is easily overcooked and dries out if left unwatched, so brush it with oil and watch it.
Barbecuing: food is cooked by radiant heat on a grid over burning charcoal or gas flames, which adds a smoky flavour.
notes.tip: Grilling's principle is radiation. For a dry-method answer, say it is digestible and quick but easily overcooked.

notes.b: Baking and roasting both use the dry heat of the oven, so the principle is convection: hot air circulating around the food.
points: Baking: food is cooked by the dry heat of the oven, transferred by convection. Fish may be baked whole, in fillets, or wrapped in foil or paper to keep it moist.
Roasting: food is cooked in a little fat in a roasting tin in the oven, by convection. It is suited to firm whole fish or thick pieces.

notes.b: Frying cooks fish in hot fat or oil. It gives a crisp surface and good flavour, but adds fat.
points: Shallow frying: food is cooked in hot fat in a pan on the hob, with heat transferred by conduction through the fat. The surface is crisp and cooking is quick, but it adds fat and calories.

Deep frying: food is immersed in hot fat in a deep fat fryer, with heat transferred by convection in the fat. A coating of batter or breadcrumbs seals the fish, keeps it moist and makes it crisp, but the result is high in fat.
Stir-frying: small pieces are cooked quickly in a wok in a small amount of oil, by conduction and convection.

notes.h: Microwave cooking and choosing a method
notes.b: Microwaves cook fish quickly with no added fat. A comparison of methods lets you comment on how palatable the cooked fish will be.
points: Microwave cooking is quick and needs no fat, but it may cook unevenly, so cover the dish and allow standing time for the heat to spread through the fish.
Grilled fish is quick, low in fat and digestible, but easily overcooked.
Poached fish is digestible and moist, but may lack flavour, so it is served with a sauce.
Fried fish is crisp and flavourful, but higher in fat and less suitable for low-fat diets.
notes.tip: For a question to name three methods and explain how one is carried out, choose from baking, grilling, roasting, frying, steaming, microwave, poaching, stewing and barbecuing, then give the method, how it is done and its principle. For a recommended dry and moist method, give the principle and comment on palatability: grilling (radiant heat, seals the surface, digestible but easily overcooked) and poaching (80-90 °C, conduction and convection, digestible but may lack flavour so serve with a sauce).

keyTerms.definition: The setting of fish protein when heated, so that the flesh turns opaque and firms.
The transfer of heat from molecule to molecule through a solid or a liquid in contact with the food.
The transfer of heat through circulating liquid, steam or hot air, in which hot material rises and cooler material falls.
The transfer of heat by infrared rays travelling in straight lines from a heat source to the food.
A moist method of cooking food gently in liquid kept just below simmering point.
A moist method of cooking food in steam rising from boiling water.
A dry method of cooking food by radiant heat from a grill, which seals the surface of the food.
Cooking food quickly by electromagnetic waves that make the water molecules in it vibrate and generate heat.

factCards.term: Three effects of cooking on fish protein
factCards.definition: The protein sets and turns opaque; the flesh firms and flakes; and the protein becomes easier to digest.

factCards.term: Three moist methods of cooking fish
factCards.definition: Poaching, steaming and stewing or casserole cooking.

factCards.term: Four dry methods of cooking fish
factCards.definition: Grilling, barbecuing, baking and shallow frying.

factCards.term: Two nutrients lost when fish is cooked in liquid
factCards.definition: Some B vitamins and minerals pass into the cooking liquid, which can be used in a sauce.

questions.prompt: Explain how heat changes the protein in fish during cooking, and why overcooking spoils the texture of the fish.
questions.model: Heat causes the protein to coagulate, so the flesh turns from translucent to opaque and firms. The connective tissue between the muscle segments breaks down, so the flesh flakes. Protein becomes easier to digest. Overcooking toughens the protein and squeezes out moisture, so the flesh becomes dry and tough.

questions.prompt: Describe two dry and two moist methods of cooking fish, naming the principle of heat transfer used in each, and comment on the palatability of the cooked fish.
questions.model: Dry methods: grilling uses radiant heat from the grill; the heat seals the surface and retains flavour, moisture and nutrients, but the fish is easily overcooked and dried. Shallow frying uses conduction through hot fat in a pan on the hob; the fish browns and develops flavour but absorbs fat. Barbecuing uses radiant heat over charcoal or gas flames; baking uses convection in the oven. Moist methods: poaching cooks fish in liquid just below simmering point, around 85 °C, using convection and conduction; the fish stays moist and digestible but may lack flavour, so it is served with a sauce. Steaming uses convection from steam rising from boiling water, retaining moisture and nutrients. Stewing or casserole cooking uses convection and conduction in liquid in a covered container. Palatability: fish cooked by dry methods has more flavour and colour but can be dry if overcooked; fish cooked by moist methods is tender and moist but can taste bland; both are digestible when cooked through.
